title: Safety Data Sheets
summary: Manufacturers, distributors, and importers must provide a Safety Data Sheet for each hazardous chemical, in a uniform 16-section format. Employers must make SDSs readily accessible to employees.
talking_points: An SDS must come with each hazardous chemical, in a uniform format with 16 numbered sections and set headings.
Section 1 gives the product identifier, supplier contact, emergency phone number, and recommended and restricted uses.
Section 2 lists the hazards and required label elements. Section 3 lists ingredients.
Section 4 has first-aid measures and symptoms. Section 5 covers fire-fighting. Section 6 covers accidental release and cleanup.
Section 7 covers safe handling and storage, including incompatibilities.
Section 8 lists exposure limits, engineering controls, and PPE. Sections 9, 10, and 11 cover physical and chemical properties, stability and reactivity, and toxicology.
OSHA does not enforce Sections 12 through 15, because other agencies regulate that information.
Employers must make sure SDSs are readily accessible to employees.
site_hazards_to_check: SDS binder or file missing, out of date, or locked away
Chemicals on site with no matching SDS
Workers who do not know where SDSs are kept
SDS not in the uniform 16-section format
Emergency phone number not known for the chemical
discussion_questions: Where are the SDSs for our chemicals, and can everyone reach them?
Which SDS section do you check for first aid, and which for spills?
What would you look up on the SDS before starting work with a new product?
